questions.title: S3 Fundamentals — Buckets, Objects and URLs
questions.question: How does AWS S3 work and how do you integrate it with a Spring Boot application for file storage?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- S3: object storage — not a file system, not a database; flat key-value store of objects
- Bucket: globally named container per region; object: key + data + metadata
- Object keys look like paths but S3 is flat — no real directories
- Storage classes: Standard, Infrequent Access, Glacier — cost/retrieval tradeoffs
- Access: IAM policies, bucket policies, ACLs (deprecated), presigned URLs
- Durability: 11 nines (99.999999999%) — data replicated across multiple AZs
- Consistency: strong read-after-write consistency since Dec 2020

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
S3 is object storage — you store files as objects identified by a key within a bucket. Unlike a file system, there are no real directories. Keys just look like paths using slashes, but they're actually flat. The bucket name must be globally unique across all AWS accounts and regions.

For a Spring Boot application, the main use cases are storing user uploads like profile pictures and documents, storing application-generated files like PDF reports, and serving static assets. Files uploaded to S3 can be made publicly accessible via their URL, or kept private and accessed via presigned URLs that give temporary access without requiring AWS credentials.

S3 durability is 11 nines — AWS replicates every object across at least three AZs within the region. You almost never need to think about data loss with S3. What you do need to think about is access control, versioning for important files, and lifecycle policies to move old files to cheaper storage classes automatically.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: S3 is object storage — you store files as objects identified by a key within a bucket.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: What you do need to think about is access control, versioning for important files, and lifecycle policies to move old files to cheaper storage classes automatically.

questions.title: S3 Security and Access Control
questions.question: How do you secure S3 buckets and control access to objects in a production Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Block Public Access: enable for all buckets by default — critical baseline
- Bucket Policy: resource-based policy controlling who can access the bucket
- IAM role for EC2/ECS: grants application permission to specific buckets
- Presigned URLs: grant time-limited access to specific objects without making bucket public
- Server-side encryption: SSE-S3 (AWS managed keys) or SSE-KMS (customer managed)
- Versioning: protect against accidental deletion — enables recovery
- S3 Access Logs / CloudTrail: audit who accessed what objects

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The most important S3 security baseline is enabling Block Public Access on every bucket. This prevents any bucket policy or ACL from accidentally making objects publicly readable. You should enable this account-wide as a Service Control Policy so no one can accidentally create a public bucket.

For application access, use IAM roles attached to your EC2 instances or ECS task roles. The application never needs AWS access keys — the SDK automatically reads credentials from the instance metadata. The role should have minimal permissions — only the specific S3 actions on the specific bucket your app uses.

For serving private files to end users, the pattern is presigned URLs. Your backend verifies the user is authenticated and authorized to access the file, generates a presigned URL with a short expiry — 5 to 15 minutes — and returns it to the client. The client downloads directly from S3 using that URL. This keeps the file private while giving authenticated users temporary access, and offloads all the bandwidth from your application servers to S3.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: The most important S3 security baseline is enabling Block Public Access on every bucket.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This keeps the file private while giving authenticated users temporary access, and offloads all the bandwidth from your application servers to S3.

questions.title: S3 Multipart Upload for Large Files
questions.question: How do you handle large file uploads to S3 efficiently from a Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Multipart upload: split large file into parts, upload in parallel, S3 assembles
- Required for files > 5GB; recommended for files > 100MB
- Advantages: retry individual parts on failure, parallel upload, pause and resume
- Transfer Manager: high-level SDK wrapper that handles multipart automatically
- Presigned multipart: allow clients to upload large files directly to S3
- Abort incomplete multipart uploads: lifecycle rule to clean up orphaned parts
- Minimum part size: 5MB (except last part)

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For files larger than 100MB, multipart upload is the right approach. You split the file into chunks — typically 8 to 16 megabytes each — upload each part independently and in parallel, then tell S3 to assemble them in the correct order. The benefit is that if one part fails to upload, you only retry that part, not the entire file. You can also parallelize uploads, which significantly reduces total upload time on a good network.

The AWS SDK provides a Transfer Manager that handles all the multipart complexity for you. You just give it a file or input stream and it automatically decides when to use multipart upload, how many parts to create, and how to run them in parallel.

For client-side large file uploads where the file comes from a browser, the recommended pattern is presigned multipart upload. The backend generates presigned URLs for each part, the browser uploads directly to S3 in parallel, and then calls your backend to complete the multipart upload. This avoids routing gigabytes of data through your application servers.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: For files larger than 100MB, multipart upload is the right approach.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: This avoids routing gigabytes of data through your application servers.

questions.title: S3 Event Notifications and Triggers
questions.question: How do you use S3 event notifications to trigger processing when files are uploaded?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- S3 Events: ObjectCreated, ObjectRemoved, etc. — triggers SNS, SQS, or Lambda
- Use case: file uploaded → process it (resize image, parse CSV, trigger workflow)
- S3 → SQS → Spring Boot consumer: decoupled, retryable, scalable
- S3 Event notification filter: only notify on specific prefixes or suffixes
- EventBridge: more powerful event routing — filter by metadata, replay events
- At-least-once delivery — idempotent processing required

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
S3 event notifications fire whenever something happens in your bucket — an object is created, deleted, or restored. You can route these events to SNS, SQS, or Lambda. For a Spring Boot application, the typical pattern is S3 to SQS to your consumer — the event goes into a queue, your consumer processes it, and if processing fails the message is retried automatically.

The common use case is processing uploaded files: a user uploads a CSV file to S3, the ObjectCreated event fires, your Spring Boot consumer receives the SQS message with the bucket and key, downloads the file from S3, processes it, and saves the results to the database. The queue provides buffering so a burst of uploads doesn't overwhelm your processing capacity.

Because S3 events have at-least-once delivery, your processing must be idempotent. If the consumer crashes after processing but before acknowledging the SQS message, the message is redelivered and your processor runs again. Use the S3 object key as an idempotency key to detect and skip already-processed files.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: S3 event notifications fire whenever something happens in your bucket — an object is created, deleted, or restored.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Use the S3 object key as an idempotency key to detect and skip already-processed files.

questions.title: S3 Lifecycle Policies and Cost Optimization
questions.question: How do you manage S3 storage costs using lifecycle policies and storage class transitions?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Lifecycle policies: automatically transition or expire objects based on age or count
- Transition: move from Standard to Standard-IA after 30 days, Glacier after 90 days
- Expiration: automatically delete objects after N days or N versions
- Intelligent-Tiering: automatically moves objects between tiers based on access patterns
- Requester Pays: bucket owner doesn't pay for data transfer costs
- Reduce data transfer costs: use CloudFront in front of S3 for frequently accessed public content
- Batch Operations: bulk actions on millions of objects

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
S3 charges for storage volume, API requests, and data transfer out of AWS. Lifecycle policies automate cost optimization by moving older data to cheaper storage classes automatically. A typical policy for a logs bucket might keep files in Standard for 7 days for quick access, transition to Standard-IA for 30 days, then transition to Glacier, and finally delete after 365 days. This is all automatic and requires no application code changes.

For frequently changing access patterns, Intelligent-Tiering is the laziest optimization — you put objects there and S3 automatically moves them between access tiers based on their actual access frequency. No lifecycle rules to define, no guessing. The only downside is a monthly monitoring fee per object, so it's not cost-effective for very small objects.

For serving frequently accessed content publicly, put CloudFront in front of S3. CloudFront caches content at edge locations close to users and eliminates data transfer out charges from S3 — you pay cheaper CloudFront data transfer rates instead, and your S3 gets far fewer API requests.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Lifecycle Policy via CloudFormation

```yaml
# CloudFormation snippet
Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
Properties:
  BucketName: app-user-uploads
  VersioningConfiguration:
    Status: Enabled
  LifecycleConfiguration:
    Rules:
      - Id: transition-and-expire
        Status: Enabled
        Transitions:
          - TransitionInDays: 30
            StorageClass: STANDARD_IA
          - TransitionInDays: 90
            StorageClass: GLACIER_IR
        ExpirationInDays: 365  # delete after 1 year

      - Id: clean-old-versions
        Status: Enabled
        NoncurrentVersionExpiration:
          NoncurrentDays: 30  # keep old versions for 30 days, then delete

      - Id: abort-incomplete-multipart
        Status: Enabled
        AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload:
          DaysAfterInitiation: 7
```

## Storage Class Costs (approximate, us-east-1)

| Class | Storage/GB/month | Min Duration | Retrieval |
|-------|-----------------|--------------|----------|
| Standard | $0.023 | None | Free |
| Standard-IA | $0.0125 | 30 days | $0.01/GB |
| Glacier Instant | $0.004 | 90 days | $0.03/GB |
| Glacier Flexible | $0.0036 | 90 days | $0.01/GB + time |
| Deep Archive | $0.00099 | 180 days | $0.02/GB + hours |

## Spring Boot: Upload with Storage Class Hint

```java
public void uploadWithStorageClass(String key, byte[] content, StorageClass storageClass) {
    PutObjectRequest req = PutObjectRequest.builder()
        .bucket(bucketName)
        .key(key)
        .storageClass(storageClass)  // StorageClass.STANDARD, STANDARD_IA, etc.
        .build();
    s3Client.putObject(req, RequestBody.fromBytes(content));
}

// For archived reports: upload directly to Glacier
uploadService.uploadWithStorageClass(
    "reports/annual/2023.pdf", pdfBytes, StorageClass.GLACIER_IR
);
```

questions.title: S3 Pre-Signed URLs and Secure Direct Uploads
questions.question: How do you implement direct browser-to-S3 uploads using pre-signed URLs in Spring Boot?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Pre-signed URL: temporary signed URL granting specific S3 permission — no AWS credentials needed in browser
- Use case: browser uploads directly to S3 — bypasses your server (no bandwidth cost on server)
- Flow: browser requests upload URL from backend → backend signs it → browser PUTs directly to S3
- Pre-signed PUT URL: for upload; GET URL: for download of private objects
- Expiry: short duration (1-15 minutes) — reduces exposure window
- Content type restriction: sign for specific content type to prevent malicious uploads
- CORS on S3 bucket: required for browser cross-origin PUT requests
- Post-upload callback: send SNS/SQS notification or use S3 event to trigger processing

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Pre-signed URLs let you grant temporary access to S3 operations without exposing AWS credentials. The backend generates a URL that is signed with your AWS credentials and includes the target bucket, key, HTTP method, content type, and expiry time. The browser then makes the HTTP request directly to S3 using that URL — S3 validates the signature and allows or denies based on the encoded permissions.

This pattern is better than proxying files through your server for two reasons. First, it eliminates server bandwidth costs for large file uploads — a user uploading a 100MB video doesn't use any of your server's network. Second, it's more scalable — S3 handles the upload directly without consuming a thread or connection on your application server.

The expiry time should be short — enough for the user to start the upload, typically 5-15 minutes. A short window limits the risk if a signed URL is intercepted. For download pre-signed URLs on private objects, keep expiry even shorter for sensitive files, or use S3's CloudFront signed URLs for content delivery.

speakable_v2.hook: Pre-signed URLs let you grant temporary access to S3 operations without exposing AWS credentials.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: For download pre-signed URLs on private objects, keep expiry even shorter for sensitive files, or use S3's CloudFront signed URLs for content delivery.
